title: Model Validation, Diagnostics and Reproducibility
objectives: Design out-of-sample and walk-forward validation schemes that respect the time ordering of data
Run core diagnostic checks on a fitted model, residual autocorrelation, distribution tails, parameter stability, benchmark comparison, and interpret a degradation ratio
Explain what reproducibility requires in a modelling pipeline: seeds, data versioning, environment pinning and one-command reruns
Recognise validation red flags such as in-sample/out-of-sample performance gaps
motivation: A model that performs beautifully on the data it was built on is not evidence of anything, it may simply have memorised. Validation is the adversarial discipline of trying to break your own model before the market does, and reproducibility is what makes the whole exercise trustworthy: a result no one can rerun is a result no one should believe.

blocks.md: The author of a model is its worst validator: you know which choices flattered the fit. So invert the instinct, the goal of a validation pass is to *break* the model cheaply, in the lab, rather than expensively in production. Two distinct questions get confused constantly: **calibration quality** (does it fit the data I gave it?) and **predictive validity** (does it forecast data it never saw?). Only the second one pays.

A useful habit is to write the validation report *before* running it: which split scheme, which benchmarks, which degradation threshold counts as failure, and what happens if the model fails (shelve, simplify, or collect more data). Pre-committing the criteria removes the temptation to reinterpret a bad number after the fact, the same pre-registration logic that disciplines hypothesis testing applies here, one level up: the hypothesis under test is '*this model generalises*'.
For cross-sectional data you can shuffle into train/validation/test. For time series you cannot: shuffling leaks the future into the past. The honest scheme keeps the arrow of time:

**Walk-forward** extends this: roll the window forward (train on years 1-3, test on year 4; train on years 2-4, test on year 5; ...), giving a sequence of out-of-sample results that mimics live operation and exposes regime dependence. The numbers should scare you when they should: a hypothetical model with in-sample $R^2 = 0.72$ collapsing to $0.11$ out of sample, or an in-sample Sharpe of $2.1$ shrinking to $0.4$, is not 'unlucky', the gap is the overfitting measured directly.

blocks.caption: Even the out-of-sample number is an estimate: an OOS $R^2$ of $0.11$ with a wide confidence band says the model may have no genuine signal at all.

items: **Residual autocorrelation**: if errors still carry memory (Ljung-Box style checks on the ACF), the mean model is incomplete, the same 'residuals must be white noise' bar from ARIMA and GARCH diagnostics.
**Heteroscedasticity**: errors whose size varies with regime suggest a variance model is missing (ARCH effects in squared residuals).
**Distribution tails**: a QQ plot bending away from the line at the extremes means normal-ish assumptions understate crash risk.
**Parameter stability**: refit on rolling windows; a parameter that jumps between windows was fitting noise.
**Benchmark comparison**: the model must beat the naive benchmark (random walk, historical mean) out of sample, sophistication that cannot beat 'tomorrow equals today' is cost.

blocks.title: Reading a degradation ratio
items: Degradation ratio: $2.9/1.2 \approx 2.42$ - predictions are $2.4\times$ worse where it counts.
Interpretation thresholds (rule of thumb, not law): $\lesssim 1.3$ - healthy; $1.3$-$2$ - investigate; $> 2$ - suspect overfitting or a regime the model never saw.
Follow up: refit with fewer parameters, check which windows drive the damage, and look for structural change near the split.

blocks.title: The tuning-set trap
blocks.md: Every time you look at validation results and change the model, the validation set is being trained on. After many such iterations its 'out-of-sample' status is spent, which is why the test set exists, is touched once, and why walk-forward re-rolling is the honest substitute for repeated peeking.
A result a colleague cannot rerun is not a result. The requirements are mundane and non-negotiable:

items: **Seeds**: every stochastic step, simulation, resampling, optimiser initialisation, takes an explicit, logged seed.
**Data versioning**: the exact input snapshot (date, query, hash) is recorded with the result; 'the database' is not a dataset.
**Environment pinning**: library versions are frozen and recorded, because dependency drift silently changes results.
**Deterministic pipeline order**: one script, one command, from raw snapshot to final table, no copy-pasted notebooks in the middle.
**Logged parameters**: every fitted value, threshold and manual override is written down with the run.

blocks.code:
import random

SEED = 20240317          # logged alongside the result
random.seed(SEED)
DATA_SNAPSHOT = "prices-2023-12-29.parquet"   # versioned input

# ... deterministic pipeline: fit, validate, report ...
# rerunning with (SEED, DATA_SNAPSHOT) reproduces every number exactly
blocks.caption: The reproducibility contract in four lines: fixed seed, named snapshot, deterministic path, logged parameters.

blocks.md: Reproducibility also compounds across a team: a seed-pinned, versioned pipeline turns a private result into a reviewable artefact, lets a second engineer rerun the analysis before a decision meeting, and makes every discrepancy diagnosable down to the exact commit and snapshot that changed. Teams that skip it do not merely lose trust, they lose the ability to learn from their own past runs, because the inputs to those runs no longer exist.

blocks.title: Why desks care more than universities
blocks.md: In production quant work, an unrepeatable backtest cannot be reviewed, an irreproducible risk number cannot be reconciled, and an audit trail is a regulatory expectation. Reproducibility is not academic virtue, it is the licence to operate.

guidedExercise.prompt: A model's in-sample RMSE is $1.2$ and its out-of-sample RMSE is $2.9$. (a) Compute the degradation ratio and classify it against the rule of thumb in the lesson. (b) The team then recomputes OOS RMSE excluding one unusual regime window and gets $1.4$. State what this reveals and what the correct response is (and is not).
hints: Ask whether the excluded window is part of the world the model must live in.
Deleting inconvenient data is not validation.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $2.9/1.2 \approx 2.42$ - above the $>2$ threshold: suspect overfitting or an unseen regime. (b) It reveals the damage is concentrated in one regime the model cannot handle, which is *the* informative failure, not noise to be trimmed. The correct response is to treat regime reliability as a requirement (add regime features, stress-test, or state the model's operating range honestly). The wrong response is shipping the $1.4$ number: excluding the hard window is redefining the test, and the live environment will not agree to exclude it.

independentExercise.prompt: A regression coefficient is re-estimated on four rolling windows, giving $\beta = 0.77, 0.81, 1.42, 0.79$. (a) Compute the mean across all four windows. (b) Recompute excluding the suspicious window. (c) Interpret the pair of numbers, and list three reproducibility requirements that would let a reviewer re-run this analysis.
hints: Sum the four values and divide by 4.
Sum the remaining three and divide by 3.
Think seeds, data snapshots, environment versions.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $(0.77 + 0.81 + 1.42 + 0.79)/4 = 3.79/4 = 0.9475$. (b) $(0.77 + 0.81 + 0.79)/3 = 2.37/3 = 0.79$. (c) The stable-window estimate $0.79$ matches the fit windows, so the $1.42$ window is an outlier regime or a fitting artefact, parameter instability that diagnostics must flag, not average away. Reviewer requirements: (1) a fixed seed for any stochastic step; (2) the versioned data snapshot with hash; (3) pinned library versions plus a one-command rerun script.

commonMistakes: Shuffling time-ordered data into random train/test splits, leaking the future into training.
Reusing the validation set for repeated model iterations and then quoting its numbers as out-of-sample.
Treating a big in-sample/out-of-sample gap as bad luck instead of the direct measurement of overfitting that it is.
Running pipelines without seeds or data versioning, then being unable to explain a changed result a week later.
realWorldApplication: Any production forecasting system, demand, credit, staffing, goes through the same gate: walk-forward evaluation against a naive benchmark, diagnostic checks on residuals, and a reproducible pipeline that risk and audit teams can rerun.
quantFinanceApplication: Backtests are validated exactly this way: walk-forward windows, comparison against a buy-and-hold or random-walk benchmark, stability of fitted factor loadings across windows, and a seed-pinned, data-versioned rerun path for every reported number.
summary: Only out-of-sample, time-respecting evaluation (holdout and walk-forward) measures predictive validity; in-sample fit measures memory.
IS/OOS gaps are the measurement of overfitting: $R^2$ $0.72 \to 0.11$ or Sharpe $2.1 \to 0.4$ is a red flag, not bad luck.
Diagnostics interrogate residuals: autocorrelation, heteroscedasticity, tail behaviour, parameter stability across windows, and superiority over the naive benchmark.
Reproducibility needs explicit seeds, versioned data snapshots, pinned environments and one-command reruns, it is the credibility layer of any quant claim.

quiz.prompt: For a time-ordered dataset, which validation split is sound?
options: Randomly shuffle all observations, then split 70/30
Train on the earliest data, validate on the middle, test on the most recent
Train and test on the same window, quoting in-sample RMSE
Validate on data that overlaps the training period
quiz.explanation: Time ordering must be preserved or the model trains on the future; random shuffling and overlapping splits both leak. In-sample numbers measure fit, not forecasting.

quiz.prompt: In-sample RMSE is $1.2$, out-of-sample RMSE is $2.9$. What is the degradation ratio (two decimals)?
Which diagnostics belong in a validation pass? Select all that apply.
options: ACF of the residuals (Ljung-Box style checks)
QQ plot of residuals for tail behaviour
Parameter estimates re-run on rolling windows
Increase of in-sample $R^2$ after adding a parameter
quiz.explanation: Residual memory, tail shape and parameter stability are diagnostic evidence; in-sample $R^2$ climbing with an extra parameter is not, it happens by construction.

quiz.prompt: Why is the test set touched only once, at the end?
quiz.modelAnswer: Each time validation results drive a model change, information leaks into the model, so repeatedly used validation data stops being out-of-sample; a test set touched once gives an honest final estimate of live performance.
quiz.explanation: Iterating against any set makes it training data in disguise; the untouched test set is the only honest reporter.

quiz.prompt: A sophisticated forecasting model achieves OOS RMSE 2.9 while the naive random-walk benchmark achieves 2.7 on the same period. The correct conclusion is:
options: The model is valuable because it is more sophisticated
The model has not beaten the naive benchmark, so its complexity is not justified yet
The comparison is invalid because the models differ
RMSE cannot be compared across models
quiz.explanation: The naive benchmark defines the bar; failing to clear it means the sophistication currently adds cost and risk without adding accuracy.

quiz.prompt: Rolling-window estimates of a coefficient are $0.77, 0.81, 1.42, 0.79$. What is their mean excluding the $1.42$ window (two decimals)?
quiz.explanation: $(0.77 + 0.81 + 0.79)/3 = 2.37/3 = 0.79$ - the outlier window is the instability signal, and should be investigated rather than averaged in.

flashcards.back: Roll the training window forward through time, testing on the following segment each step, mimics live operation and exposes regime dependence.
Any information from the evaluation period (or its labels/statistics) influencing training, including statistics computed before the split.
Residual ACF, heteroscedasticity, QQ tails, rolling parameter stability, and outperformance of the naive benchmark.
Explicit seeds + versioned data snapshot + pinned environment + one-command deterministic rerun, all logged with the result.
